subject: chemistry

items.q: When sodium compounds are heated in a flame, the flame turns yellow. Which process in the sodium atoms produces this yellow light?
items.correct: Excited electrons fall to lower energy levels, emitting photons.
items.misconception: Electrons absorb energy and emit photons as they rise to higher levels.
items.why: The events happen together in a flame or discharge tube (the atoms are energized and light appears), so students attach the emission to the step they are told about first, the excitation. Absorption and emission are also easily confused because both involve the same energy levels. Separate the two steps. Excitation: the electron gains energy (from heat or an electric discharge) and moves up. Emission: the electron falls back to a lower level and the energy difference leaves as a photon. An emission line therefore corresponds to a downward transition.
items.specStatementText: Emission spectra are produced by atoms emitting photons when electrons in excited states return to lower energy levels.
items.random_wrong: Electrons escape from the atoms entirely, releasing energy as photons.

items.q: Violet light and red light lie at opposite ends of the visible spectrum. How does violet light compare with red light?
items.correct: Violet photons carry more energy, as violet light has the higher frequency.
items.misconception: Violet light has the lower frequency, as it has the shorter wavelength.
items.why: Both are numbers describing a wave, and 'more' of one is assumed to mean 'more' of the other. The inverse relationship is often met only as an equation, not as a picture. All electromagnetic radiation travels at the same speed in a vacuum, so if the waves are longer, fewer of them pass a point each second. Shorter wavelength means higher frequency, and higher frequency means higher photon energy.
items.specStatementText: Emission spectra are produced by atoms emitting photons when electrons in excited states return to lower energy levels.
items.random_wrong: Violet light has the longer wavelength, as its photons carry more energy.

items.q: White light from a hot filament lamp gives a continuous spectrum when it is passed through a prism. Light from a hydrogen discharge tube passed through the same prism gives a line spectrum. How does the line spectrum differ from the continuous spectrum?
items.correct: It shows bright lines at only certain wavelengths, on a dark background.
items.misconception: It shows dark lines at certain wavelengths, across a continuous band of colour.
items.why: Absorption spectra (for example of the Sun) are often shown next to emission spectra, and both are called 'line spectra', so students merge the two images. An emission spectrum shows only the light the atoms give out, so it is dark except at the wavelengths emitted. An absorption spectrum shows continuous light with the wavelengths absorbed by the atoms removed.
items.specStatementText: Emission spectra are produced by atoms emitting photons when electrons in excited states return to lower energy levels.
items.random_wrong: It shows only one bright line, since a hydrogen atom has only one electron.

items.q: Consider the set of lines in the hydrogen emission spectrum produced by electrons falling to n = 2 from higher levels. Which statement about the lines in this set is correct?
items.correct: The lines get closer together towards higher frequency.
items.misconception: The lines are equally spaced in frequency across the set.
items.why: Shell diagrams draw the shells as evenly spaced circles, and the 'ladder' analogy suggests equal steps. The gap between n = 1 and n = 2 is much larger than the gap between n = 2 and n = 3, and the gaps keep shrinking as n increases. The lines of each set therefore crowd together towards higher frequency until they converge.
items.specStatementText: The line emission spectrum of hydrogen provides evidence for the existence of electrons in discrete energy levels, which converge at higher energies.
items.random_wrong: The lines get closer together towards lower frequency.

items.q: Which electron transition in a hydrogen atom emits the photon of highest frequency?
items.why: Energy-level diagrams label each level with its own energy, and students read the line off one level instead of the gap between two; this association of spectral lines with single levels rather than transitions is reported in research on students' understanding of spectra. Always take the difference: photon energy = E(upper level) − E(lower level). A fall into n = 1 involves a large difference (ultraviolet), a fall into n = 2 a smaller one (mainly visible) and a fall into n = 3 a smaller one again (infrared).
items.specStatementText: The line emission spectrum of hydrogen provides evidence for the existence of electrons in discrete energy levels, which converge at higher energies.

items.q: In the hydrogen emission spectrum, transitions ending at n = 1 produce lines in the ultraviolet region. In which region are the lines produced by transitions ending at n = 3, and why?
items.correct: Infrared, because the energy gaps from higher levels down to n = 3 are smaller than those down to n = 2
items.misconception: Ultraviolet, because the levels above n = 3 are more widely spaced than the levels above n = 2
items.why: Students transfer the spatial picture (outer shells are larger, further out) to the energy picture and assume the energy gaps widen as the shells spread out. Distance from the nucleus and energy spacing are different things. The energy gaps between levels shrink as n increases, so the lines of each set crowd together at high frequency, not at low frequency.
items.specStatementText: The line emission spectrum of hydrogen provides evidence for the existence of electrons in discrete energy levels, which converge at higher energies.
items.random_wrong: Ultraviolet, because n = 3 is a higher energy level than n = 2, so its photons carry more energy

items.q: What is the maximum total number of electrons that the first three main energy levels of an atom (n = 1, 2 and 3) can hold?
items.why:
The '2, 8, 8' rule used for the first 20 elements in earlier courses is remembered as a limit on the third shell, because the 3d sublevel does not begin to fill until after 4s. The 2, 8, 8 pattern describes the first 20 elements only. The third level holds up to 18 electrons; the 3d sublevel fills after 4s, from scandium to zinc.

Working: Maximum electrons in level n = 2n². n = 1: 2 × 1² = 2; n = 2: 2 × 2² = 8; n = 3: 2 × 3² = 18. Total = 2 + 8 + 18 = 28.
items.specStatementText: The main energy level is given an integer number, n, and can hold a maximum of 2n² electrons.
items.working: Maximum electrons in level n = 2n². n = 1: 2 × 1² = 2; n = 2: 2 × 2² = 8; n = 3: 2 × 3² = 18. Total = 2 + 8 + 18 = 28.

items.q: Which description of a 1s atomic orbital is correct?
items.correct: A spherical region centred on the nucleus where the electron is most likely to be found
items.misconception: A circular path round the nucleus along which the electron travels at a fixed distance
items.why: The planetary (Bohr) model, shell diagrams drawn as circles and the similarity of the words 'orbit' and 'orbital' all suggest a path; this is one of the most widely reported misconceptions about atomic structure. An electron in an atom cannot be given a path. An orbital describes where the electron is likely to be found: an s orbital is a sphere of high probability, a p orbital a dumbbell of high probability.
items.specStatementText: A more detailed model of the atom describes the division of the main energy level into s, p, d and f sublevels of successively higher energies.
items.random_wrong: A spherical region centred on the nucleus that contains the electron at every instant

items.q: Which description of the shapes and orientations of the three 2p atomic orbitals is correct?
items.correct: Three dumbbell shapes along the x, y and z axes, at 90° to one another
items.misconception: Three dumbbell shapes lying in one plane, at 120° to one another
items.why: Students misapply the idea that repelling electron domains spread out as far apart as possible, which gives 120° for three domains in a plane. The three p orbitals are defined along three perpendicular axes: px along x, py along y and pz along z. Each is a dumbbell with its two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus.
items.specStatementText: A more detailed model of the atom describes the division of the main energy level into s, p, d and f sublevels of successively higher energies.
items.random_wrong: Three figure-of-eight paths that the electrons follow around the nucleus

items.q: In a potassium atom, the nineteenth electron occupies the 4s sublevel rather than the 3d sublevel. What is the reason?
items.correct: The 4s sublevel is lower in energy than the 3d sublevel in this atom.
items.misconception: The 4s orbital is nearer the nucleus, and orbitals fill from the inside outward.
items.why: Shell diagrams are filled from the inner shell outwards, so filling order and distance are learned as the same thing. The filling order is decided by energy. For potassium and calcium the 4s sublevel is lower in energy than 3d, so it is filled first, even though its electrons are, on average, further from the nucleus.
items.specStatementText: A more detailed model of the atom describes the division of the main energy level into s, p, d and f sublevels of successively higher energies.
items.random_wrong: Hund’s rule requires an s sublevel to be filled before any d sublevel.

items.q: Which condensed electron configuration of a ground-state atom is correct?
items.correct: chromium: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹
items.misconception: copper: [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s²
items.why: Applying the Aufbau order mechanically works for every other element from hydrogen to krypton, so students do not expect exceptions. Learn the two exceptions: Cr [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ and Cu [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. In each, one electron that the simple rule would place in 4s is in 3d instead.
items.specStatementText: Each orbital has a defined energy state for a given electron configuration and chemical environment, and can hold two electrons of opposite spin. Sublevels contain a fixed number of orbitals, regions of space where there is a high probability of finding an electron.
items.random_wrong: potassium: [Ar] 3d¹

items.q: Which full electron configuration of a ground-state atom is correct?
items.correct: iron: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶ 4s²
items.misconception: cobalt: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁹
items.why: It seems logical to finish level 3 before starting level 4, and configurations are often written in numerical order (… 3d⁶ 4s²), which hides the order of filling. Follow the energy order: after 3p (argon) the next electrons enter 4s (potassium, calcium), and only then 3d (scandium to zinc). Potassium is [Ar] 4s¹, not [Ar] 3d¹.
items.specStatementText: Each orbital has a defined energy state for a given electron configuration and chemical environment, and can hold two electrons of opposite spin. Sublevels contain a fixed number of orbitals, regions of space where there is a high probability of finding an electron.
items.random_wrong: scandium: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 4p¹

items.q: An iron atom (Z = 26) has the condensed electron configuration [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². How is an Fe²⁺ ion formed from this atom?
items.correct: Both of the 4s electrons are removed from the atom.
items.misconception: Two of the six 3d electrons are removed from the atom.
items.why: It seems natural that the last electrons added should be the first removed, and the Aufbau order is learned without any rule for ions. Once the 3d orbitals are occupied, the 4s electrons are the higher-energy, outer electrons and are removed first. Remove 4s, then 3d: Fe → Fe²⁺ [Ar] 3d⁶ → Fe³⁺ [Ar] 3d⁵.
items.specStatementText: Each orbital has a defined energy state for a given electron configuration and chemical environment, and can hold two electrons of opposite spin. Sublevels contain a fixed number of orbitals, regions of space where there is a high probability of finding an electron.
items.random_wrong: One 4s electron and one 3d electron are each removed.

items.q: An orbital (arrow-in-box) diagram is drawn for a ground-state nitrogen atom, 1s² 2s² 2p³. The 1s box and the 2s box each contain two arrows pointing in opposite directions. Which description of the 2p part of the diagram is correct?
items.correct: Three boxes each hold one arrow, and all three arrows point the same way.
items.misconception: Three boxes: one holds two opposite arrows, one holds one, one is empty.
items.why: The s sublevels, met first, have a single orbital that simply fills with a pair, and students copy this box-by-box filling onto p and d sublevels. For p and d sublevels, place one arrow in each box first, all pointing the same way, then add second arrows pointing the opposite way. Nitrogen’s 2p³ has three singly occupied boxes.
items.specStatementText: Each orbital has a defined energy state for a given electron configuration and chemical environment, and can hold two electrons of opposite spin. Sublevels contain a fixed number of orbitals, regions of space where there is a high probability of finding an electron.
items.random_wrong: Three boxes each hold one arrow, and the middle arrow is reversed.

items.q: What is the maximum number of electrons that a 3d sublevel can hold, and why?
items.correct: 10 electrons, as its five orbitals can each hold two electrons of opposite spin
items.misconception: 20 electrons, as its ten orbitals can each hold two electrons of opposite spin
items.why:
The electron capacities 2, 6, 10 and 14 are memorized and then remembered as the numbers of orbitals. Halve the capacity to get the number of orbitals: s 2 → 1 orbital, p 6 → 3, d 10 → 5, f 14 → 7. Each orbital holds two electrons of opposite spin.

Working: A d sublevel has 5 orbitals; each orbital holds a maximum of 2 electrons (opposite spins). Maximum = 5 × 2 = 10 electrons.
items.specStatementText: Each orbital has a defined energy state for a given electron configuration and chemical environment, and can hold two electrons of opposite spin. Sublevels contain a fixed number of orbitals, regions of space where there is a high probability of finding an electron.
items.random_wrong: 18 electrons, as the n = 3 energy level holds a maximum of 2n² electrons
items.working: A d sublevel has 5 orbitals; each orbital holds a maximum of 2 electrons (opposite spins). Maximum = 5 × 2 = 10 electrons.

items.q: In the emission spectrum of hydrogen, the set of lines produced by electrons falling to n = 1 has its lowest-frequency line at a wavelength of 121.6 nm and converges to a limit at a wavelength of 91.18 nm. What is the first ionization energy of hydrogen? (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹; N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹; E = hf; c = λf)
items.correct: 1312 kJ mol⁻¹
items.misconception: 983.8 kJ mol⁻¹
items.why:
The first line is the most prominent and the n = 2 → n = 1 transition is the one most often drawn, so students take it to represent removing the electron from n = 1. Moving the electron from n = 1 to n = 2 only excites it. Removing it means taking it to n = ∞, whose energy corresponds to the convergence limit at the highest frequency (shortest wavelength) of the set.

Working: The convergence limit of the set ending at n = 1 corresponds to ionization from the ground state. f = c/λ = (2.998 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) ÷ (91.18 × 10⁻⁹ m) = 3.288 × 10¹⁵ s⁻¹. E = hf = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)(3.288 × 10¹⁵ s⁻¹) = 2.179 × 10⁻¹⁸ J per atom. Per mole: 2.179 × 10⁻¹⁸ J × 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 1.312 × 10⁶ J mol⁻¹ = 1312 kJ mol⁻¹ (4 significant figures, matching the data; this agrees with the accepted value, 1312 kJ mol⁻¹).
items.specStatementText: In an emission spectrum, the limit of convergence at higher frequency corresponds to ionization.
items.random_wrong: 1.312 × 10⁶ kJ mol⁻¹
items.working: The convergence limit of the set ending at n = 1 corresponds to ionization from the ground state. f = c/λ = (2.998 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) ÷ (91.18 × 10⁻⁹ m) = 3.288 × 10¹⁵ s⁻¹. E = hf = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)(3.288 × 10¹⁵ s⁻¹) = 2.179 × 10⁻¹⁸ J per atom. Per mole: 2.179 × 10⁻¹⁸ J × 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 1.312 × 10⁶ J mol⁻¹ = 1312 kJ mol⁻¹ (4 significant figures, matching the data; this agrees with the accepted value, 1312 kJ mol⁻¹).

items.q: How does the first ionization energy change from lithium to sodium to potassium in group 1, and why?
items.correct: It decreases, as the outer electron is in a higher main level, further out and more shielded.
items.misconception: It decreases, as the fixed pull of the nucleus is shared among a larger number of electrons.
items.why: Students treat the attraction like a resource that is used up; this 'conservation of force' idea is reported in chemistry-education research on ionization energy. Each electron is attracted by the nucleus according to the nuclear charge and its distance, reduced by shielding from inner electrons. Removing one electron does not release 'spare' attraction for the others.
items.specStatementText: In an emission spectrum, the limit of convergence at higher frequency corresponds to ionization.
items.random_wrong: It increases, as the nuclear charge rises from +3 to +19 and attracts the electron more strongly.

items.q: How does the first ionization energy generally change across period 3 from sodium to argon, and why?
items.correct: It increases, as the nuclear charge rises while the outer electrons have similar shielding.
items.misconception: It decreases, as the atoms get larger because more electrons are added along the period.
items.why: More particles are assumed to take up more space, as with everyday objects. Across a period, nuclear charge increases while shielding stays similar, so the outer electrons are pulled closer. Oxygen atoms are smaller than nitrogen atoms, and period 3 atoms shrink from sodium to argon.
items.specStatementText: In an emission spectrum, the limit of convergence at higher frequency corresponds to ionization.
items.random_wrong: It decreases, as the fixed pull of the nucleus is shared among more and more electrons.

items.q: The first ionization energies (kJ mol⁻¹) of the period 2 elements are: Li 520, Be 900, B 801, C 1086, N 1402, O 1314, F 1681, Ne 2081. Which statement correctly explains both the fall from Be to B and the fall from N to O?
items.correct: B’s electron is in 2p, higher in energy than 2s; O’s is in a doubly occupied 2p orbital, where repulsion raises its energy.
items.misconception: Be’s filled 2s sublevel and N’s half-filled 2p sublevel have a special stability that makes them harder to ionize.
items.why: The phrase 'half-filled and filled sublevels are especially stable' is widespread in textbooks and on websites and seems to explain the anomalies neatly. Compare the energies of the electrons removed. For N and O, write 2p³ (three unpaired) and 2p⁴ (one orbital paired); the paired electron in O is repelled by its partner and is removed more easily.
items.specStatementText: In an emission spectrum, the limit of convergence at higher frequency corresponds to ionization.
items.random_wrong: B’s electron is in a doubly occupied 2p orbital, where repulsion raises its energy; O’s is in a higher sublevel than N’s.

items.q: The first four successive ionization energies of an element X are 578, 1817, 2745 and 11 577 kJ mol⁻¹. In which group of the periodic table is X?
items.correct: Group 13, as the large increase comes after the third electron is removed
items.misconception: Group 14, as the large increase appears at the fourth ionization energy
items.why: Students count to the first large value in the list and read off its position, one place too far. Find the jump between two values, IEₙ and IEₙ₊₁. The number of outer electrons is n, the number removed before the jump; the group is n for n = 1 or 2, and 10 + n for n = 3 to 8.
items.specStatementText: Successive ionization energy (IE) data for an element give information about its electron configuration.
items.random_wrong: Group 1, as the second value is already over three times larger than the first

items.q: The first four successive ionization energies of sodium are 496, 4562, 6910 and 9543 kJ mol⁻¹. Which explanation of the large increase from the first to the second value is correct?
items.correct: The second electron is removed from the 2p sublevel, which is closer to the nucleus and less shielded.
items.misconception: The Na⁺ ion has a stable noble-gas octet, and ions resist losing electrons from a complete outer shell.
items.why: The octet rule is taught early to predict formulas, and the language of atoms 'wanting' electrons turns it into a cause; this 'octet framework' is widely reported in chemistry-education research. Explain every ionization energy by the energy of the electron removed: how strongly it is attracted, given the nuclear charge, its distance from the nucleus and the shielding by inner electrons.
items.specStatementText: Successive ionization energy (IE) data for an element give information about its electron configuration.
items.random_wrong: After one electron is lost, the fixed pull of the nucleus is shared among 10 electrons, not 11.

items.q: Which of these condensed electron configurations of ground-state atoms is correct?
items.correct: copper: [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹
items.misconception: chromium: [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s²
items.why: Applying the Aufbau order mechanically works for every other element from hydrogen to krypton, so students do not expect exceptions. Learn the two exceptions: Cr [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ and Cu [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. In each, one electron that the simple rule would place in 4s is in 3d instead.
items.specStatementText: Each orbital has a defined energy state for a given electron configuration and chemical environment, and can hold two electrons of opposite spin. Sublevels contain a fixed number of orbitals, regions of space where there is a high probability of finding an electron.
items.random_wrong: scandium: [Ar] 3d³

items.q: A potassium atom (Z = 19) has the electron arrangement 2, 8, 8, 1: two electrons in the first main energy level, eight in the second, eight in the third and one in the fourth. Which statement about the third main energy level (n = 3) of this atom is correct?
items.correct: It is not full, because a level with n = 3 can hold up to 2 × 3² = 18 electrons.
items.misconception: It is not full, because it has n² = 9 orbitals and so has room for one more electron.
items.why:
Hund’s rule (electrons occupy orbitals singly first) and diagrams with one arrow per box are read as a maximum of one electron per orbital. Hund’s rule describes the order in which orbitals of equal energy are occupied, not their capacity. The Pauli exclusion principle allows two electrons, of opposite spin, in every orbital.

Working: Maximum number of electrons in main energy level n = 2n². For n = 3: 2 × 3² = 18. The third level of potassium holds 8 of a possible 18, so it is not full; the nineteenth electron enters the fourth level (4s) because 4s is lower in energy than 3d, not because the third level is full.
items.specStatementText: The main energy level is given an integer number, n, and can hold a maximum of 2n² electrons.
items.random_wrong: It is full, because every main energy level after the first holds a maximum of 8 electrons.
items.working: Maximum number of electrons in main energy level n = 2n². For n = 3: 2 × 3² = 18. The third level of potassium holds 8 of a possible 18, so it is not full; the nineteenth electron enters the fourth level (4s) because 4s is lower in energy than 3d, not because the third level is full.

items.q: The diagram shows part of the emission spectrum of hydrogen plotted against frequency. The four lines P, Q, R and S lie in the visible region, and the lines converge towards the limit marked L. Which electron transition produces line P?
items.why:
Students transfer the idea that a bigger water wave is more powerful; wave diagrams with a long wavelength look larger. For electromagnetic radiation, photon energy depends on frequency, and frequency is inversely related to wavelength. Violet light, with a shorter wavelength than red, has a higher frequency and a higher photon energy.

Working: Visible lines of hydrogen arise from transitions ending at n = 2. Photon energy E = hf, so the lowest-frequency line P is the smallest energy gap ending at n = 2, i.e. n = 3 → n = 2. Higher starting levels give higher-frequency lines that converge on L (n = ∞ → n = 2).
items.specStatementText: The line emission spectrum of hydrogen provides evidence for the existence of electrons in discrete energy levels, which converge at higher energies.
items.working: Visible lines of hydrogen arise from transitions ending at n = 2. Photon energy E = hf, so the lowest-frequency line P is the smallest energy gap ending at n = 2, i.e. n = 3 → n = 2. Higher starting levels give higher-frequency lines that converge on L (n = ∞ → n = 2).

items.q: The diagram shows four arrow-in-box diagrams, W, X, Y and Z, each drawn for the 3d sublevel of a ground-state iron atom, [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². Which diagram is correct?
items.correct: Diagram X
items.misconception: Diagram Y
items.why: The Pauli exclusion principle ('opposite spins') is remembered without its condition, 'in the same orbital', and applied to every pair of electrons. The opposite-spin requirement applies within one orbital. Across the orbitals of one sublevel, singly occupied orbitals have parallel spins: in nitrogen all three 2p arrows point the same way.
items.specStatementText: Each orbital has a defined energy state for a given electron configuration and chemical environment, and can hold two electrons of opposite spin. Sublevels contain a fixed number of orbitals, regions of space where there is a high probability of finding an electron.
items.random_wrong: Diagram W

items.q: The graph shows log₁₀ of the successive ionization energies of an element plotted against the number of electrons removed. In which group of the periodic table is the element?
items.correct: Group 14, because the first large jump comes after four electrons have been removed
items.misconception: Group 12, because the largest jump on the graph comes after the twelfth electron
items.why:
The rule of thumb ‘look for the big jump’ is remembered without the word ‘first’, and on a log plot the later jump into the n = 1 level is often the largest one drawn. Count the electrons removed before the FIRST large jump: those are the outer electrons. For a period 3 element the second, larger, jump after the twelfth electron only marks the start of the n = 1 level.

Working: Read the graph: the points rise gently for electrons 1–4, then jump between the 4th and 5th values (the first large jump). Four electrons are removed before the jump, so the element has four outer electrons (ns² np²): group 14. The second jump between the 12th and 13th values marks the two n = 1 electrons, so the element has 14 electrons in total and is silicon.
items.specStatementText: Successive ionization energy (IE) data for an element give information about its electron configuration.
items.random_wrong: Group 15, because the first large jump is seen at the fifth ionization energy

items.q: Is the light in an emission spectrum produced by electrons leaving the atom?
items.correct: No. Emission lines are produced by electrons moving between energy levels within the atom. The electron stays in the atom and falls to a lower level, emitting a photon.
items.misconception: Atoms give out light when electrons are knocked out of them completely; the light is the energy released as the electrons escape.
items.why: Everyday talk of energy being 'given off' when something is released, and the high temperatures of flames and discharge tubes, lead students to picture electrons being driven out of atoms. Excitation (moving to a higher level) and ionization (removal) are often not distinguished in early teaching. Excitation moves an electron to a higher level inside the atom; ionization removes it. Removing an electron requires energy; it does not release light. The lines of an emission spectrum come from electrons falling back to lower levels of the same atom.
items.specStatementText: Emission spectra are produced by atoms emitting photons when electrons in excited states return to lower energy levels.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the colour of a flame or discharge tube the colour of the atoms themselves?
items.correct: No. Individual atoms have no colour. The colour is the light emitted as photons of particular energies when excited electrons fall to lower energy levels.
items.misconception: Each kind of atom has its own colour, and hot atoms glow with that colour.
items.why: Students attribute the properties of a substance, such as colour, to its individual particles; this transfer of macroscopic properties to atoms is widely reported in chemistry-education research. Colour is a property of the light reaching the eye. Sodium light is yellow because the most intense sodium emission lines have wavelengths near 589 nm, which correspond to one particular energy difference between levels.
items.specStatementText: Emission spectra are produced by atoms emitting photons when electrons in excited states return to lower energy levels.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is red the highest-energy colour of visible light?
items.correct: No. Red light has the lowest photon energy in the visible spectrum; violet has the highest.
items.misconception: Red light is the most energetic visible light, because red is the colour of hot, energetic things.
items.why: Everyday colour conventions link red with heat and danger (red-hot metal, red hot taps, warning signs) and blue with cold. Order the visible spectrum by energy: red (lowest), orange, yellow, green, blue, violet (highest). Infrared, beyond red, has even lower photon energy; ultraviolet, beyond violet, has higher.
items.specStatementText: Emission spectra are produced by atoms emitting photons when electrons in excited states return to lower energy levels.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is each line in the hydrogen spectrum produced by a different electron?
items.correct: No. A hydrogen atom has only one electron. Each line corresponds to a different transition between two energy levels; a sample contains very many atoms, whose electrons make different transitions.
items.misconception: Each spectral line comes from a different electron in the atom, so the number of lines equals the number of electrons.
items.why: Students link the lines to particles they can count rather than to transitions between levels, and are not reminded that a sample contains very many atoms. The hydrogen spectrum has many lines even though each atom has one electron. In a sample, different atoms have their electrons falling between different pairs of levels at the same moment, and each kind of transition gives one line.
items.specStatementText: The line emission spectrum of hydrogen provides evidence for the existence of electrons in discrete energy levels, which converge at higher energies.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a sublevel the same thing as one orbital?
items.correct: No. A sublevel is a set of orbitals of equal energy: an s sublevel has one orbital, a p sublevel three, a d sublevel five and an f sublevel seven. Each orbital holds up to two electrons.
items.misconception: Each sublevel (s, p, d, f) is a single orbital, so each sublevel holds just one pair of electrons.
items.why: The words shell, sublevel and orbital are used loosely and sometimes interchangeably, and the first sublevels met (1s, 2s) are single orbitals holding one pair, so every sublevel is pictured the same way. Picture the hierarchy: main level → sublevels → orbitals → at most two electrons per orbital. The 2p sublevel consists of three separate orbitals, 2px, 2py and 2pz.
items.specStatementText: A more detailed model of the atom describes the division of the main energy level into s, p, d and f sublevels of successively higher energies.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the electron always inside the boundary drawn for an orbital?
items.correct: No. The boundary drawn for an orbital encloses the region where there is a high probability of finding the electron; the probability outside it is small but not zero.
items.misconception: The electron is confined inside the drawn surface of its orbital, so it is inside that region at every moment.
items.why: Orbital diagrams show a sharp outline, and students read the outline as a container. An orbital is a region of high probability. Drawings use a surface that encloses most (not all) of the probability, so the electron is most likely, not certain, to be inside it.
items.specStatementText: A more detailed model of the atom describes the division of the main energy level into s, p, d and f sublevels of successively higher energies.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do electrons sit at fixed points in an atom, as drawn in shell diagrams?
items.correct: No. The positions of electrons in an atom cannot be fixed; an orbital describes the probability of finding an electron in a region around the nucleus.
items.misconception: Electrons are held at fixed points around the nucleus, as the dots and crosses in shell diagrams show.
items.why: Dot-and-cross and shell diagrams place electrons at definite points, and students read the drawing convention literally. The dots and crosses are a counting device, not positions. Two electrons in a 1s orbital are both described by the same spherical region of high probability.
items.specStatementText: A more detailed model of the atom describes the division of the main energy level into s, p, d and f sublevels of successively higher energies.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does Hund’s rule set the order in which sublevels are filled?
items.correct: No. The order of filling (lowest energy first) is the Aufbau principle. Hund’s rule deals only with how electrons occupy orbitals of equal energy within one sublevel.
items.misconception: Hund’s rule is the rule that says which sublevel fills first, such as s before p or 4s before 3d.
items.why: The three principles are learned together as a list of names, and students attach each name to the wrong idea. Aufbau: fill the lowest-energy orbitals first. Pauli: at most two electrons per orbital, with opposite spins. Hund: within a sublevel, singly occupy each orbital with parallel spins before pairing.
items.specStatementText: Each orbital has a defined energy state for a given electron configuration and chemical environment, and can hold two electrons of opposite spin. Sublevels contain a fixed number of orbitals, regions of space where there is a high probability of finding an electron.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do other atoms and ions rearrange their electrons to reach a half-filled (3d⁵) or filled (3d¹⁰) d sublevel, as chromium and copper do?
items.correct: No. Chromium and copper are the only exceptions for atoms up to Z = 36. Other atoms follow the regular order (Ni is [Ar] 3d⁸ 4s²), and transition-metal ions are formed by removing 4s electrons first (Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶).
items.misconception: Half-filled and filled d sublevels are so favoured that any atom or ion arranges its 4s and 3d electrons to reach 3d⁵ or 3d¹⁰ wherever it can.
items.why: The Cr and Cu exceptions are often explained by a 'special stability' of half-filled and filled sublevels, and a stated reason invites students to apply it wherever 3d⁵ or 3d¹⁰ can be reached. Treat Cr and Cu as learned exceptions, not as a rule to extend. Write other configurations by the Aufbau order, and form transition-metal ions by removing the 4s electrons first.
items.specStatementText: Each orbital has a defined energy state for a given electron configuration and chemical environment, and can hold two electrons of opposite spin. Sublevels contain a fixed number of orbitals, regions of space where there is a high probability of finding an electron.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a positive ion form by gaining electrons?
items.correct: No. A positive ion forms when an atom loses electrons. Fe²⁺ has two electrons fewer than an Fe atom (24 instead of 26).
items.misconception: A positive charge means extra has been added, so a 2+ ion has gained two electrons.
items.why: In everyday language 'positive' and 'plus' mean an addition, so students forget that the added particles would be negatively charged electrons. Electrons are negative. Losing two electrons leaves two more protons than electrons, a charge of 2+. Gaining two electrons gives a 2− ion.
items.specStatementText: Each orbital has a defined energy state for a given electron configuration and chemical environment, and can hold two electrons of opposite spin. Sublevels contain a fixed number of orbitals, regions of space where there is a high probability of finding an electron.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can one sublevel hold as many electrons as its whole main energy level (2n²)?
items.correct: No. The 2n² rule gives the capacity of a whole main energy level, shared among its sublevels. For n = 3, the 18 electrons are distributed as 3s², 3p⁶ and 3d¹⁰.
items.misconception: The 3d sublevel can hold 2n² = 18 electrons, because it belongs to the n = 3 level.
items.why: Configurations write the level number and the sublevel letter together (3d), so students apply the rule for the level to the sublevel. Separate level and sublevel: n = 3 holds 18 in total; its d sublevel holds 10 (five orbitals × 2).
items.specStatementText: Each orbital has a defined energy state for a given electron configuration and chemical environment, and can hold two electrons of opposite spin. Sublevels contain a fixed number of orbitals, regions of space where there is a high probability of finding an electron.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is an energy calculated in J mol⁻¹ already in kJ mol⁻¹?
items.correct: No. E = hf gives joules; after multiplying by the Avogadro constant the energy is in J mol⁻¹, and it must be divided by 1000 to give kJ mol⁻¹.
items.misconception: The number obtained from E = hf × N_A can be written directly with the unit kJ mol⁻¹ asked for in the question.
items.why: The Planck constant is in J s, so the calculation produces joules, but ionization energies are always quoted in kJ mol⁻¹; students copy the unit from the question without converting. Track the unit through each step: J per atom → (× N_A) J mol⁻¹ → (÷ 1000) kJ mol⁻¹. A first ionization energy of order 10⁶ kJ mol⁻¹ is far too large; values for the elements up to Z = 36 range from 419 kJ mol⁻¹ (potassium) to 2372 kJ mol⁻¹ (helium).
items.specStatementText: In an emission spectrum, the limit of convergence at higher frequency corresponds to ionization.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does ionization energy depend only on nuclear charge?
items.correct: No. Nuclear charge is one factor; the distance of the electron from the nucleus and the shielding by inner electrons also matter. Down a group the increases in distance and shielding outweigh the increase in nuclear charge.
items.misconception: More protons always mean a stronger attraction, so the ionization energy rises whenever the nuclear charge rises.
items.why: Nuclear charge is the easiest factor to read from the periodic table, so it is used on its own. Weigh all three factors. From Li (+3) to K (+19) the outer electron moves from n = 2 to n = 4, much further out and shielded by more inner electrons, so the first ionization energy falls.
items.specStatementText: In an emission spectrum, the limit of convergence at higher frequency corresponds to ionization.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can the change-of-sublevel explanation and the electron-pairing explanation be used for either discontinuity in first ionization energy across period 2?
items.correct: No. Each explanation belongs to one discontinuity. Be → B: boron’s single 2p electron is in a higher-energy sublevel than beryllium’s 2s electrons. N → O: both lose a 2p electron, but oxygen’s comes from a doubly occupied orbital, where repulsion raises its energy.
items.misconception: Either explanation (a new, higher sublevel or paired electrons) can be used for either discontinuity.
items.why: The two discontinuities are learned together, and the two explanations are memorized without being linked to the orbital occupancy of the atoms concerned. Write the outer configurations: Be 2s², B 2s² 2p¹ (new sublevel); N 2s² 2p³, O 2s² 2p⁴ (same sublevel, one orbital now paired). The configuration shows which explanation applies.
items.specStatementText: In an emission spectrum, the limit of convergence at higher frequency corresponds to ionization.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does any large rise in successive ionization energies show a change of main energy level?
items.correct: No. Successive ionization energies always rise, because each electron is removed from a more positive ion. The change of main level is shown by an increase much larger than the others, typically several times the neighbouring increases.
items.misconception: Any clear rise between successive ionization energies, such as the second being three times the first, marks the removal of an electron from a new inner level.
items.why: Students expect successive ionization energies of electrons in one level to be almost equal, so every rise looks like a jump. Compare the rises. For X: 578 → 1817 → 2745 rises steadily, then 2745 → 11 577 increases about fourfold. Only the last is the big jump, so X has three outer electrons.
items.specStatementText: Successive ionization energy (IE) data for an element give information about its electron configuration.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is an element with three outer electrons in group 3?
items.correct: No. In the 1–18 numbering used by the IB, an element with three outer electrons (ns² np¹) is in group 13. Group 3 contains scandium and yttrium, which are d-block elements.
items.misconception: The group number equals the number of outer electrons, so three outer electrons means group 3.
items.why: The older numbering (groups I–VIII) matched group number to outer electrons for all main-group elements, and many resources still use it. For the p block, add 10 to the number of outer electrons: three outer electrons → group 13, four → group 14. Groups 1 and 2 are unchanged.
items.specStatementText: Successive ionization energy (IE) data for an element give information about its electron configuration.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does removing an electron increase the nuclear charge?
items.correct: No. The nuclear charge depends only on the number of protons, which does not change when an ion forms. Na and Na⁺ both have a nuclear charge of +11.
items.misconception: When an atom loses an electron, its nuclear charge rises (for example from +11 to +12 for Na⁺), so the remaining electrons are held more tightly.
items.why: The charge of the ion (+1) is confused with the charge of the nucleus, and the symbol Na⁺ is read as a change in the nucleus. Ionization changes only the number of electrons. The large increase between the first and second ionization energies of sodium arises because the second electron is removed from the 2p sublevel of a lower main level, closer to the nucleus and less shielded.
items.specStatementText: Successive ionization energy (IE) data for an element give information about its electron configuration.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does E = hf give the energy for one mole of atoms?
items.correct: No. E = hf gives the energy of one photon, which is the energy needed for one atom; multiplying by the Avogadro constant gives the energy per mole.
items.misconception: The energy from E = hf is already the energy per mole, so it can be converted to kJ mol⁻¹ without multiplying by the Avogadro constant.
items.why: Ionization energies are always quoted per mole, and the energy from E = hf is not recognized as the energy of a single photon, and so of a single atom; the unit kJ mol⁻¹ is attached to it directly. Track what each number refers to: E = hf is per photon, which ionizes one atom. Multiply by the Avogadro constant (N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹) to get J mol⁻¹, then divide by 1000 for kJ mol⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: In an emission spectrum, the limit of convergence at higher frequency corresponds to ionization.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a p sublevel one orbital that holds all six of its electrons?
items.correct: No. A p sublevel is a set of three orbitals of equal energy, and each orbital holds up to two electrons, so the six electrons of 2p⁶ occupy three orbitals as three pairs.
items.misconception: A sublevel is a single orbital that holds all of the sublevel’s electrons together, e.g. one 2p orbital holding up to six electrons.
items.why: Configurations such as 2p⁶ show one label for the whole sublevel, and the words sublevel and orbital are used interchangeably. Picture the hierarchy: main level → sublevels → orbitals → at most two electrons per orbital. The 2p sublevel consists of three separate orbitals, 2px, 2py and 2pz, drawn as three boxes.
items.specStatementText: A more detailed model of the atom describes the division of the main energy level into s, p, d and f sublevels of successively higher energies.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can the two electrons that share one orbital have the same spin?
items.correct: No. By the Pauli exclusion principle, two electrons in the same orbital must have opposite spins, drawn in a box diagram as one up arrow and one down arrow (↑↓).
items.misconception: Hund’s rule means that all the electrons in a sublevel have parallel spins, so two electrons in the same orbital can both be drawn as up arrows (↑↑).
items.why: Hund’s rule is remembered as ‘spins parallel’ without its condition, ‘in different orbitals of the same sublevel’, so the parallel-spin idea is carried into a box that holds a pair. Hund’s rule applies to electrons in different orbitals of one sublevel. Once two electrons share one orbital, the Pauli exclusion principle requires their spins to be opposite: ↑↓, never ↑↑.
items.specStatementText: Each orbital has a defined energy state for a given electron configuration and chemical environment, and can hold two electrons of opposite spin. Sublevels contain a fixed number of orbitals, regions of space where there is a high probability of finding an electron.
